name: Vaseline on lashes/brows

lead: People dab petroleum jelly on lashes and brows as an inexpensive conditioner so the hairs look glossier and fuller. The sheen is visible right away.

Petroleum jelly forms an occlusive coating that reduces moisture loss and adds shine; it does not act on hair follicles. Lash length is largely set by genetics, and the only FDA-approved drug for lash growth is bimatoprost. No human studies in the sources tested it for growth, so claims that it grows more hair come from user reports.

paras: People apply a small amount with a clean spoolie or fingertip along lashes and brows, often at night, as part of a conditioning routine.
It can cause irritation if it gets in the eye, and some petroleum jelly products can contain trace hydrocarbons that regulators have commented on.

angle.text: People dab petroleum jelly on lashes and brows as a cheap conditioner so the hairs look glossier and fuller. The sheen shows right away. Claims that it grows more hair come from user reports; no studies tested it.

lead: Applying petroleum jelly (Vaseline is the best-known brand) to eyelashes and eyebrows is a grooming practice promoted as a way to condition hair and make lashes or brows look fuller or glossier. Petroleum jelly is a semi-solid hydrocarbon mixture widely used in skin products to reduce moisture loss.[1]

No published human studies found in the sources consulted have tested petroleum jelly for increasing lash or brow length or density. Wikipedia notes that lash length is largely set by genetics and that the only FDA-approved drug for lash growth is bimatoprost (Latisse, 2009), a prescription product.[2]
infobox: Cosmetic/OTC skin protectant; not approved for hair growth

paras: Petroleum jelly is mainly a skin protectant and occlusive, used in lotions and cosmetics to reduce moisture loss and friction.[1] Proponents of using it on lashes and brows describe it as a cheap conditioner that makes hairs look shinier and may protect them.

Wikipedia reports that lash growth is limited by genetics and that follicle number is fixed before birth, and describes prostaglandin analogs such as bimatoprost as the approved growth drug.[2] The petroleum jelly article describes it as a moisture-retaining skin protectant and does not mention lash or brow use.[1]

The petroleum jelly article notes that it can contain mineral oil aromatic hydrocarbons, and that European Food Safety Authority and consumer-testing reports raised concerns about contamination in some products.[1] Products used near the eye can cause irritation; the sources consulted give no data specific to lashes.
